name: Secrets Handling for Agents
question: Could the agent leak an API key or password?
summary: Agents call APIs and databases, so they need credentials, but anything in the model’s context can be repeated, logged or extracted by injection. Secrets therefore stay out of prompts, tool descriptions, memory and traces. The strongest pattern is a broker: the agent requests an action, a trusted service fetches the credential from a vault and makes the call, and only the result returns to the model. Credentials are short-lived and narrowly scoped where possible (dynamic database users, one-hour tokens), outputs and logs are scanned for secret patterns, and keys are rotated on any suspicion. Which user may call which tool with which scopes is covered by Tool Authentication and Scoped Permissions (module 8); this technique is about the credential material itself.
useCases: Agents calling payment gateways, databases or cloud APIs
Coding agents that run shell commands with environment variables
Any system whose prompts and traces are stored or sent to vendors

return {"status": r.json()["status"]}           # only the result goes back
# prompt, tool descriptions and memory contain no credentials

steps.title: Expose actions, not keys
steps.text: Kiran Pay, a fictional payment aggregator, gives its operations agent a settlement_status tool. The tool’s description and arguments mention no key.

steps.title: Fetch the secret in a broker
steps.text: The broker authenticates to Vault with its own workload identity, reads the gateway token, calls the API and returns only the status. The model never sees the token.

steps.title: Use dynamic credentials
steps.text: Database access uses a Vault-generated read-only user that expires in one hour. A leaked password is useless by the next shift.

steps.title: Scan what you log
steps.text: Every event is passed through secret-pattern redaction before it goes to the tracing service, so a token echoed by a tool never lands in traces.

steps.title: Keep context clean
steps.text: The system prompt, tool descriptions and memory contain no credentials, so prompt injection has nothing to extract.

steps.title: Rehearse revocation
steps.text: On suspicion, all leases under the role are revoked with one command. In red-team tests, leaked keys fall from 18 a quarter to none.

pros: Nothing for injection or the model to repeat
Short-lived credentials shrink the damage of any leak
Clean logs and traces can be shared with vendors
cons: A broker service to build and run
Vault or a cloud secret manager to operate
Dynamic credentials need apps that refresh them
avoidWhen: Keys in prompts, tool descriptions, memory or notebooks
Coding agents running in the same process or environment as production keys

practice.scenario: Kiran Pay, a fictional payment aggregator, first gave its operations agent the gateway key in the system prompt. A red team extracted it in 45% of attempts, and every trace sent to the tracing vendor contained it. Now the agent calls tools through a broker that reads credentials from Vault, database access uses one-hour dynamic users, and outputs and logs pass through secret redaction. Leaked keys fall from 18 a quarter to none, and any key that did leak would expire within an hour.

industries.use: Gateway and bank API keys used by operations agents
Coding agents working in repositories and terminals full of .env files
Agents that restart services with cloud credentials

numericDrill.question: A static key is rotated every 90 days. If it leaks at a random moment, how many hours will it keep working on average?
numericDrill.answer: On average a leak happens halfway through the rotation period: 90 ÷ 2 = 45 days × 24 = 1,080 hours. A 1-hour dynamic credential works for 30 minutes on average.

interview.question: How should an agent use an API key safely?
interview.answer: The model never holds it. Tools run through a broker that fetches the credential from a vault, makes the call and returns only the result; credentials are short-lived and narrowly scoped, and outputs and logs are scanned for secrets.

interview.question: Why is putting a key in the system prompt dangerous?
interview.answer: Anything in context can be repeated in an answer, extracted by prompt injection, and stored in every log and trace, including at vendors.

mistakes.mistake: Keys in prompts or tool descriptions
mistakes.fix: Keep them in a vault behind a broker

mistakes.mistake: Logging full prompts and tool results raw
